big_case_rationale: Decides whether a President may shut off asylum at the southern border by proclamation under 8 U.S.C. 1182(f), plus the reach of the INA's bar on classwide injunctions; a flagship immigration and executive-power case.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority holds that Proclamation 10,888's asylum bar is lawful as a matter of statutory interpretation of the INA rather than inherent Article II power: because 8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(1)(A) commits the grant of asylum to executive discretion and nothing in section 1158 requires that discretion to be exercised case by case, the Executive may categorically deny asylum to aliens who enter in violation of a section 1182(f) entry suspension, and section 1158(a)(1)'s 'may apply' language does not oblige it to process applications whose denial is foreordained; the Court rejects the D.C. Circuit's view that such a categorical bar is an eligibility limit that must be adopted by regulation under section 1158(b)(2)(C).

The majority's ground is confined to asylum, a discretionary benefit: it does not hold that section 1182(f) or section 1185(a) lets the President displace the INA's removal procedures generally, and it leaves standing the lower courts' rulings that covered aliens keep access to statutory withholding of removal and Convention Against Torture protection, so the holding reaches categorical discretionary denials of asylum tied to a section 1182(f) suspension and not a general presidential power to expel outside the statute.
